messages.subject: Comparing models across groups
parts: Hello! I know how to use the measurementInvariance() function to compare groups, I kwow that two models can be compared by the compareFit() function, but...  It is possible to compare two different models (one-factor model Vs. three-factor model) across two groups (e.g. males Vs. females)? Thank you

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Comparing models across groups
parts: It is possible to compare two different models (one-factor model Vs. three-factor model) across two groups (e.g. males Vs. females)?

You only get one set of fit measures for the model, even if it is a multiple-group model.  Perhaps all you mean is that you want a different model fit to the two groups (perhaps so you can compare it to a model with the same factor structure)?  In your case, a one-factor model is equivalent to a 3-factor model in which all factor variances are equal (ideally, just fix them all to 1) and all factor correlations are fixed to 1.  You will get a warning message that the latent covariance matrix is not positive definite (NPD), but you can ignore it because you are making it NPD on purpose.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

What do you think about this?

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Comparing models across groups
parts: if I fit the normal three-factor model, then I still have to specify a second three-factor model with the fixed correlations, and the problem remains the same. Isn't it? Or did I misunderstand you? I'm thinking to do one MG-CFA for the one-factor model and one MG-CFA for the three-factor model. Then I can compare the two outputs by hand (chi-square, AIC, etc). What do you think about this?

Perhaps I misunderstood you.  I was under the impression that you already fit a 3-factor model in a multigroup CFA (same structure for both groups, but you wanted to test the hypothesis that a single factor was sufficient in only one of the groups.  In that case, you could simply impose fix all variances and correlations among the three factors to 1, only in that particular group.  You can calculate the chi-squared difference test using the anova() or lavTestLRT() function to compare the fit of that constrained model (equivalent to 1-factor in one of the groups) to the unconstrained 3-factor model, which would test whether your hypothesis was tenable.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
